source_text: Quae cum ita sint, non existimemus ad mortuos, pro quibus curam gerimus, peruenire, nisi quod pro eis siue altaris siue orationum siue elemosynarum sacrificiis sollemniter supplicamus, quamuis non pro quibus fiunt omnibus prosint, sed eis tantum quibus dum uiuunt conparatur, ut prosint. sed quia non discernimus, qui sint, oportet ea pro regeneratis omnibus facere, ut nullus eorum praetermittatur, ad quos haec beneficia possint et debeant peruenire. melius enim supererunt ista eis, quibus nec obsunt nec prosunt, quam eis deerunt, quibus prosunt. diligentius tamen facit haec quisque pro necessariis suis, quo pro illo fiat similiter a suis. corpori autem humando quidquid inpenditur, non est praesidium salutis, sed humanitatis officium secundum affectum, quo nemo umquam carnem suam odio habet unde oportet ut quam potest pro carne proximi curam gerat. cum ille inde recesserit qui gerebat. et si haec faciunt, qui carnis resurrectionem non credunt, quanto magis debent facere qui credunt, ut corpori mortuo, sed tamen resurrecturo et in aeternitate mansuro inpensum eius modi officium sit etiam quodam modo eiusdem fidei testimonium! quod uero quisque apud memorias martyrum sepelitur, hoc tantum mihi uidetur prodesse defuncto, ut commendans eum etiam martyrum patrocinio affectus pro illo supplicationis augeatur.
thought_title: What actually reaches the dead, and why we bury at martyrs' memorials
orientation: Augustine is concluding his answer to Paulinus about burial and the dead, stating what benefits the dead and what burial itself does.
pass_a_gloss: Since these things are so, let us not think that anything reaches the dead, for whom we take care, except what we solemnly pray for them by sacrifices of the altar or of prayers or of alms, although these do not benefit all for whom they are done, but only those for whom, while they live, it is obtained that they may benefit them. But because we do not discern who they are, it is right to do these things for all the baptized, so that none of them may be passed over, to whom these benefits can and ought to reach. For these things will more readily be in excess for those whom they neither harm nor benefit, than they will be lacking for those whom they benefit. Yet each person does these things more diligently for his own dear ones, so that the same may be done for him by his own. But whatever is spent on burying a body is not a safeguard of salvation, but a service of human kindness according to the affection by which no one ever hates his own flesh; whence it is right that, as much as he can, he take care for the flesh of his neighbor, when he who bore it has departed from it. And if those who do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh do these things, how much more ought those who believe to do them, so that a service of this kind paid to a dead body, but one that is nevertheless going to rise and remain in eternity, may also be in a certain way a testimony of that same faith! But as for the fact that someone is buried at the memorial shrines of martyrs, this alone seems to me to benefit the deceased, that, commending him also to the intercession of the martyrs, the affection of prayer for him may be increased.

choices.why: The glossary gives 'sacrifice' for sacrificium, the eucharistic offering made at the altar.
The glossary gives 'the baptized' for regenerati, those born again in Christ.
The glossary gives 'memorial shrine' for memoria, and 'martyrs' for martyres.
The glossary gives 'intercession' for patrocinium, the advocacy of martyrs on behalf of the dead.
The glossary gives 'affection' for affectus, the natural human feeling or disposition.
The glossary gives 'prayer' for supplicatio, prayer of entreaty offered for the dead.

pass_b_english: Since this is so, we should not think that anything reaches the dead for whom we are caring except what we solemnly pray for them through the sacrifices of the altar, of prayers, and of alms. Yet these do not benefit all for whom they are offered, but only those for whom, while they lived, provision was made that they might benefit. But because we cannot discern who these are, we ought to offer them for all the baptized, so that none of those to whom these benefits can and should reach may be passed over. For it is better that these things be in excess for those whom they neither harm nor help than that they be lacking for those whom they help. Still, each person does these things more diligently for his own dear ones, so that the same may be done for him by his own. Whatever is spent on burying a body, however, is not a safeguard of salvation but a service of human kindness, according to the affection by which no one ever hates his own flesh. So a person ought to care as much as he can for the flesh of his neighbor when the one who bore it has departed from it. And if those who do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh do these things, how much more ought those who do believe to do them, so that this kind of service paid to a body that is dead but will rise again and remain for eternity is also in some way a testimony of that same faith! But as for being buried near the memorial shrines of martyrs, this seems to me to benefit the deceased only in this way: that by commending him also to the intercession of the martyrs, the affection of prayer for him may be increased.

problems.quote: obtained the grace that they should benefit
problems.why: 'conparatur' means 'is prepared/provided' not 'obtained the grace'; passive present, not active past.
problems.fix: is prepared so that they may benefit

edits.old: obtained the grace that they should benefit
edits.new: is prepared so that they may benefit

fixed: Changed 'obtained the grace that they should benefit' to 'is prepared so that they may benefit': source 'conparatur, ut prosint' is passive present ('is prepared/provided'), not active past 'obtained the grace'.

problems.why: "conparatur" means "is provided/acquired," not "is prepared." The sense is about what the living person acquired/obtained so that the benefits may help them after death.
problems.fix: but only those for whom, while they lived, provision was made that they might benefit

edits.old: but only those who, while they lived, is prepared so that they may benefit.
edits.new: but only those for whom, while they lived, provision was made that they might benefit.

fixed: Changed 'is prepared' to 'provision was made' to render 'conparatur' (is provided/acquired) correctly; the source says 'eis tantum quibus dum uiuunt conparatur, ut prosint' — for whom, while they live, it is obtained that they may benefit.

problems.quote: through the sacrifices of the altar, or of prayers, or of alms
problems.source_quote: siue altaris siue orationum siue elemosynarum sacrificiis
problems.why: Sacrificiis governs all three: sacrifices of altar, prayers, alms. English makes 'sacrifices' apply only to altar.
problems.fix: through the sacrifices of the altar, of prayers, and of alms
problems.ruling: sacrificiis governs all three: altar, prayers, alms; English wrongly limits 'sacrifices' to altar only

edits.old: through the sacrifices of the altar, or of prayers, or of alms
edits.new: through the sacrifices of the altar, of prayers, and of alms

fixed: Fixed: 'sacrificiis' governs all three genitives (altaris, orationum, elemosynarum), so 'sacrifices' must apply to prayers and alms as well as the altar.

last_rejected.why: "necessariis" means relatives/kin, not merely "dear ones"; kinship obligation is key.
last_rejected.ruling: necessariis suis can mean dear ones/dependents; 'dear ones' is within normal range, not a meaning-changing error.

last_rejected.source_quote: cum ille inde recesserit qui gerebat
last_rejected.why: "gerebat" means carried/bore the body as burden, not "bore" as in gave birth; "ille" is the person himself who inhabited it.
last_rejected.fix: when the one who carried it has departed from it
last_rejected.ruling: English 'bore it' correctly renders 'gerebat' as bore/carried; no birth sense implied; 'ille' = the one who departed.
